title: What are the SQL constraint types — `PRIMARY KEY`, `UNIQUE`, `NOT NULL`, `DEFAULT`, `CHECK`, `FOREIGN KEY` — and what does each enforce (entity integrity, uniqueness, mandatory value, fallback value, domain rule, referential integrity)?

s1_definition.profdef: SQL constraints are rules the database enforces on column and table data so that invalid data can never be stored, regardless of which application writes it. `PRIMARY KEY` enforces entity integrity (a unique, non-null identifier per row); `UNIQUE` enforces that a column or set of columns has no duplicate values; `NOT NULL` makes a value mandatory; `DEFAULT` supplies a fallback value when none is given; `CHECK` enforces a domain rule on the values themselves; and `FOREIGN KEY` enforces referential integrity by requiring a value to match an existing row in another table.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of these as the non-negotiable rules at National Bank of India's data desk. PRIMARY KEY is the rule that every account must have one unique account number. UNIQUE is the rule that no two customers can register the same email. NOT NULL is the rule that an account must have a holder name — you cannot leave it blank. DEFAULT is the rule that a new account starts ACTIVE unless told otherwise. CHECK is the rule that a balance can never be negative. FOREIGN KEY is the rule that a transaction must point to a real, existing account, not a made-up one.
s1_definition.oneliner: PRIMARY KEY identifies, UNIQUE forbids duplicates, NOT NULL demands a value, DEFAULT fills one in, CHECK validates the value, and FOREIGN KEY ties rows to real parents — all enforced by the database itself.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** SQL constraints are rules the database enforces on column and table data so that invalid data can never be stored, regardless of which application writes it. `PRIMARY KEY` enforces entity integrity (a unique, non-null identifier per row); `UNIQUE` enforces that a column or set of columns has no duplicate values; `NOT NULL` makes a value mandatory; `DEFAULT` supplies a fallback value when none is given; `CHECK` enforces a domain rule on the values themselves; and `FOREIGN KEY` enforces referential integrity by requiring a value to match an existing row in another table.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of these as the non-negotiable rules at National Bank of India's data desk. PRIMARY KEY is the rule that every account must have one unique account number. UNIQUE is the rule that no two customers can register the same email. NOT NULL is the rule that an account must have a holder name — you cannot leave it blank. DEFAULT is the rule that a new account starts ACTIVE unless told otherwise. CHECK is the rule that a balance can never be negative. FOREIGN KEY is the rule that a transaction must point to a real, existing account, not a made-up one.

**One line to remember:** PRIMARY KEY identifies, UNIQUE forbids duplicates, NOT NULL demands a value, DEFAULT fills one in, CHECK validates the value, and FOREIGN KEY ties rows to real parents — all enforced by the database itself.

sections.s2_technical:
PRIMARY KEY enforces entity integrity. It marks the column or set of columns that uniquely identifies each row; it is implicitly both UNIQUE and NOT NULL, and a table has at most one primary key. The engine builds an index on it, which also makes lookups by key fast.

UNIQUE enforces that no two rows share the same value in the constrained column or combination of columns. Unlike a primary key you can have several unique constraints on a table, and a unique column may allow nulls (how nulls interact with uniqueness varies slightly by database, but typically multiple nulls are permitted). It too is backed by an index.

NOT NULL makes the value mandatory: an insert or update that leaves the column null is rejected. This is how you guarantee a field like holder_name is always present.

DEFAULT supplies a fallback value when an insert does not provide one. It does not reject anything; it fills the gap, for example setting status to ACTIVE or created_at to the current timestamp automatically.

CHECK enforces a domain rule — a boolean condition on the row's own values that must hold, such as balance greater than or equal to zero, or status being one of a fixed set. The engine rejects any insert or update that would make the condition false.

FOREIGN KEY enforces referential integrity: a value in the child table must match an existing value (usually a primary key) in a parent table, so a transaction cannot reference a non-existent account. Foreign keys also define what happens to children when the parent changes or is deleted, via ON DELETE / ON UPDATE actions like CASCADE, RESTRICT, or SET NULL.

The senior nuance is that constraints belong in the database because they are the last line of defence shared by every application, every script, and every direct SQL session. Application-only validation can be bypassed, can race under concurrency, and is duplicated across services; a database constraint is enforced once, atomically, for everyone. The trade-off is a small write-time cost and the need to handle constraint-violation errors gracefully in code.
sections.s3_banking:
The real problem: National Bank of India must guarantee that account and transaction data is always valid no matter which service writes it.

Problem 1 — every account needs a unique identity and a mandatory name. PRIMARY KEY on account id and NOT NULL on holder name enforce this.

Problem 2 — no duplicate emails, sensible defaults, and no negative balance. UNIQUE on email, DEFAULT on status and balance, and CHECK on balance enforce these.

Problem 3 — a transaction must reference a real account. FOREIGN KEY from transactions to accounts enforces referential integrity, and an invalid reference is rejected.

The code models a ConstraintedStore that checks each constraint on insert and rejects violations, an AccountService and TransactionService that go through it, and a demo attempting several valid and invalid writes to show each constraint firing.

##### 4b. SQL Database Script

```sql
-- V1__create_tables.sql (Flyway) — every constraint type demonstrated
CREATE TABLE accounts (
    id          VARCHAR(20) PRIMARY KEY,                 -- entity integrity
    holder_name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,                   -- mandatory value
    email       VARCHAR(100) UNIQUE,                     -- no duplicates
    status      VARCHAR(10)  NOT NULL DEFAULT 'ACTIVE',  -- fallback value
    balance     DECIMAL(15,2) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0.00
                CHECK (balance >= 0)                     -- domain rule
);

CREATE TABLE transactions (
    txn_id     BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
    account_id VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL
               REFERENCES accounts(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,  -- referential integrity
    amount     DECIMAL(15,2) NOT NULL CHECK (amount > 0)
);

INSERT INTO accounts (id, holder_name, email, balance) VALUES
    ('SAV2001','Rajesh Kumar','rajesh@nbi.in', 1000000.00),
    ('CUR3001','Priya Sharma','priya@nbi.in', 250000.00);
```

##### 4c. Configuration File

```yaml
# application.yml
spring:
  jpa:
    hibernate:
      ddl-auto: validate   # trust the DB constraints; never let Hibernate rewrite them
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input: a series of account and transaction writes, some valid and some violating each constraint.

Step 1 — The first account is inserted with a null status, so the DEFAULT rule fills it with ACTIVE. The id is unique, the holder name is present, the email is new, and the balance is non-negative, so every constraint passes and the row is stored.

Step 2 — A second insert reuses id SAV2001, violating the PRIMARY KEY uniqueness; it is rejected.

Step 3 — An insert with a null holder name violates NOT NULL and is rejected. An insert reusing Rajesh's email violates UNIQUE and is rejected. An insert with a negative balance violates CHECK and is rejected.

Step 4 — A transaction for the existing SAV2001 passes the FOREIGN KEY and amount CHECK, so it is stored. A transaction for a non-existent account violates the FOREIGN KEY and is rejected. Each constraint has now visibly protected the data.

Final output:

```
2026-10-25 17:43:00 [INFO] account inserted: SAV2001 status=ACTIVE
2026-10-25 17:43:00 [SEVERE] duplicate PRIMARY KEY → REJECTED: PRIMARY KEY duplicate: SAV2001
2026-10-25 17:43:00 [SEVERE] NOT NULL violated (no holder name) → REJECTED: NOT NULL violated: holder_name
2026-10-25 17:43:00 [SEVERE] UNIQUE email violated → REJECTED: UNIQUE violated: rajesh@nbi.in
2026-10-25 17:43:00 [SEVERE] CHECK balance<0 violated → REJECTED: CHECK violated: balance < 0
2026-10-25 17:43:00 [INFO] transaction inserted for SAV2001 amount=50000
2026-10-25 17:43:00 [SEVERE] FOREIGN KEY violated (no such account) → REJECTED: FOREIGN KEY violated: no account NOPE9999
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  INSERT account / transaction
    │
    ▼
  Database constraint gauntlet (all enforced at write time)
    ├─ PRIMARY KEY   → id unique & non-null?      no → REJECT
    ├─ NOT NULL      → holder_name present?        no → REJECT
    ├─ UNIQUE        → email not duplicate?         no → REJECT
    ├─ DEFAULT       → status missing? fill ACTIVE
    ├─ CHECK         → balance >= 0 / amount > 0?   no → REJECT
    └─ FOREIGN KEY   → account_id exists in parent? no → REJECT
    │ all pass
    ▼
  Row stored (guaranteed valid for EVERY writer)
```

```
  │  Guard/validation chain: each constraint a gate            │
  │  Defensive invariants at the data boundary                 │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  │  S: ConstraintedStore enforces; services orchestrate.      │

  ┌──────────────────────────┐        ┌───────────────────────┐
  │ ConstraintedStore        │───────▶│ Account               │
  │ - accounts: Map (PK)     │ stores │ - id/holderName/email │
  │ - emails: Set (UNIQUE)   │        │ - status/balance      │
  │ + insertAccount(a)       │        └───────────────────────┘
  │ + insertTransaction(...) │  FK + CHECK on transactions
  └──────────────────────────┘

  ── Call Chain ──
  1. insertAccount(status=null) → DEFAULT fills ACTIVE → stored
  2. insertAccount(dup id)      → PK reject
  3. insertAccount(null name)   → NOT NULL reject
  4. insertAccount(dup email)   → UNIQUE reject
  5. insertAccount(bal<0)       → CHECK reject
  6. insertTransaction(SAV2001) → FK ok → stored
  7. insertTransaction(NOPE)    → FK reject
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
SQL constraints are rules the database itself enforces so that invalid data can never be stored, no matter which application, batch job, or direct SQL session does the writing. There are six core types and each enforces one thing. PRIMARY KEY enforces entity integrity: it is the unique, non-null identifier for each row, implicitly both unique and not-null, and a table has at most one. UNIQUE enforces that a column or combination of columns has no duplicate values, and a table can have several unique constraints. NOT NULL makes a value mandatory, rejecting any insert or update that leaves the column empty. DEFAULT does not reject anything; it quietly supplies a fallback value when the insert gives none, like setting a new account's status to ACTIVE or stamping the created time. CHECK enforces a domain rule — a boolean condition on the row's own values, such as balance being at least zero or status being one of a fixed set — and rejects anything that would make it false. FOREIGN KEY enforces referential integrity: a value in the child table must match an existing row in a parent table, so a transaction cannot point to an account that does not exist, and it also controls what happens to children on parent delete or update.

The reason I put these in the database rather than only in application code is that the database is the last line of defence shared by everyone. Application validation can be skipped by a different service, bypassed by a migration script or a direct SQL session, and it can race under concurrency; a database constraint is enforced once, atomically, for every writer. The small price is a write-time cost and the need to catch constraint-violation errors and turn them into clean responses.

In our National Bank of India schema, the account id is a PRIMARY KEY, holder name is NOT NULL, email is UNIQUE, status DEFAULTs to ACTIVE, a CHECK forbids a negative balance, and every transaction has a FOREIGN KEY to a real account. When a batch feed once tried to insert a transaction for a non-existent account, the foreign key rejected it at the database rather than silently corrupting the ledger, and when two signups raced on the same email the unique constraint stopped the duplicate that the application check had missed. The line I remember is that PRIMARY KEY identifies, UNIQUE forbids duplicates, NOT NULL demands a value, DEFAULT fills one in, CHECK validates the value, and FOREIGN KEY ties rows to real parents — all enforced by the database itself for every writer.
